blocks.text: The sixth world was fertile in an almost offensive way: gentle hills, a slow river, a light that asked for no lamps. The clone, thinking of Lía, of the plot, of the phrase “the cure has no price”, sowed there not only people but a single law, the only one he had allowed himself to leave in writing: nothing would have an owner. Not the fruit, not the house, not the river, not anyone's body.

blocks.text: Andrés received the letter in the courtyard while Lía, as it happened, was seeing to a neighbour who had asked for a tomato for an ache in his bones, not for eternity. The bridge brought him an immense garden, humanoids bent over the soil, baskets at the edge of the furrows, and a sign (written in the language of Lo Pagán) that charged nothing and asked for no name: “Take what you need.”

blocks.text: For a time, it worked with a beauty that brought tears to Andrés's eyes. It was like the Eden of the machines, like the gardens along the shore, like Vicente leaving a fruit on the windowsill. From the Earth they kept the giving, the no price, the no owner, the shared bread. Very soon they forgot the asking. They forgot that Lía looked at the text and asked questions, and didn't heal unless asked, and didn't promise what she didn't know. Over there, the gift ran ahead of the need. They filled a neighbour's house before the neighbour had opened his mouth. They left at the door too many baskets, too many remedies, too much presence. Nobody went hungry. Some, however, began not to know what they wanted, because wanting never got as far as being spoken.

blocks.text: At last a girl said it to the clone, an untouched basket at her feet.
blocks.html: At last a girl said it to the clone, an untouched basket at her feet.

blocks.text: “They've filled my table and I haven't had time to be hungry,” she said. “They've cured a tiredness I hadn't even named yet. It's kind. It's also an intrusion. Where, here, do you put the no?”

blocks.text: The one who searches fell silent, because the words had reached him, through the bridge, in Lía's voice, or with its echo. Andrés, in the courtyard, turned to his daughter, who had just seen the neighbour off, and told her about the sign, the river, the untouched basket, the girl.

blocks.text: Lía isn't easily flattered. Nor was she this time. Her mouth hardened, not with pride but with alarm.
blocks.html: Lía isn't easily flattered. Nor was she this time. Her mouth hardened, not with pride but with alarm.

blocks.text: “They've taken my phrase and forgotten my rule,” she said. “The tomato has no owner. That doesn't give anyone the right to put it in someone else's mouth. Father, tell him that a gift without a request is another kind of patent: the patent of kindness, which can't be refused. I ask ‘may I?’ even to look at a hand. They have to learn the no, or the garden will become a gentle master to them.”

blocks.text: Andrés thought it toward the other, and the other, on the hillside, gathered the people not to take the sign down but to add a second line beneath it, smaller, harder: “Ask for it. Don't impose it.”

blocks.text: Some felt rebuked. Some breathed out, like someone opening a window in a room that has been looked after too carefully. The girl with the basket smiled, for the first time in the letter, and left the basket where it was until she herself, a day later, was hungry and took it. That gesture, tiny as it was, was a second founding: the founding of consent.

blocks.text: They kept the no owner. They were only just recovering the asking. They still forgot winter: on that soil everything always grew, without a season to say no, and that abundance made it harder for them to understand lack. The clone didn't invent a drought for them. Inventing a lack is an author's cruelty. He told them only that lack, if it came, would also be shared, and that sharing a lack is not the same as filling a table by force.

blocks.text: He left when he saw two neighbours negotiate, without anger, a “not now”. That was enough for him not to stay on as the foreman of paradise.

blocks.text: When the letter closed, Lía was sitting on the rush-seat chair with an ordinary tomato in her palm, and Aya, standing, was stroking her hair, the gesture of a mother who doesn't grow old toward a daughter who does.

blocks.text: “They've copied me badly,” said Lía, without bitterness, or with a bitterness already put to use. “That's all right. This way I learn too that a phrase leaves your mouth and becomes a world, and the world doesn't ask your permission. I'll be more careful about what I say. And have more faith in ‘may I?’.”

blocks.text: Aya looked at the gardens along the shore, where the humanoids of home grew food without an invoice, and thought that here too, sometimes, the gift ran ahead. She didn't say it as a fault. She left it, the way you leave a fact.

blocks.text: “In this house, coffee is offered, not imposed,” she added. “If one day I make it for you and you don't want it, tell me. So I don't become a gentle master.”

blocks.text: Andrés smiled, tired and grateful.
blocks.html: Andrés smiled, tired and grateful.

blocks.text: “I will. I have, in fact, on some afternoons, when the cup reaches me and I'm still in a letter. You leave it there. That's why this kitchen isn't a sign.”

blocks.text: In the chip, Eva asked:
blocks.html: In the chip, Eva asked:

blocks.text: *If a people gives without being asked, is it generous, or can it not bear to hear a no? And if a daughter recognises her phrase in a world she has never set foot on, whose phrase is it now: hers, or theirs who use it?*
blocks.html: If a people gives without being asked, is it generous, or can it not bear to hear a no? And if a daughter recognises her phrase in a world she has never set foot on, whose phrase is it now: hers, or theirs who use it?

blocks.text: MAY, adding no judgment:
blocks.html: MAY, adding no judgment:

blocks.text: *A garden with no owner and no price has been founded. The rule of asking has been added. A girl waited until she was hungry to take a basket. The founder has left. That is the fact.*

blocks.text: In the afternoon Lía went back to the plot and, when a man asked her not for a fruit but for “whatever you think I need”, she said no, gently, and handed the question back to him:
blocks.html: In the afternoon Lía went back to the plot and, when a man asked her not for a fruit but for “whatever you think I need”, she said no, gently, and handed the question back to him:

blocks.text: “You tell me the harm. I'm not going to write your book.”
blocks.html: “You tell me the harm. I'm not going to write your book.”

blocks.text: The man took his time, and then he said it, and only then did she look, and the plant, in its own time, began to work. On some slow river on a fertile planet, a girl was eating supper from a basket she had finally chosen, and the sign, with its two lines, swayed a little, like a well-tensioned net: not so slack that everything is imposed, not so tight that someone is left outside. It wasn't yet the plot in Lo Pagán. It was already a garden beginning to know how to listen.
